questions.question: A 'repetition maximum' (RM), as first described by DeLorme, is defined as:

options.A: The greatest amount of weight a muscle can move through full available ROM a specific number of times before fatiguing
options.B: The maximum number of exercise sessions a patient can complete in a week
options.C: The total duration in months of a resistance training program
options.D: A measure of joint range of motion only

questions.explanation: A repetition maximum (RM) is the greatest amount of weight (load) a muscle can move through the full available range of motion, with control, a specific number of times before fatiguing — e.g. a '10-RM' is the maximum weight that can be lifted through 10 repetitions.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: Why is establishing a 1-RM (single maximum effort) considered inappropriate for certain patient populations, such as those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology?

options.A: It takes too long to administer in a clinical setting
options.B: It requires a single maximal effort, which carries risk for patients with joint impairments, healing soft tissue, osteoporosis, or cardiovascular pathology
options.C: It is only valid for measuring endurance, not strength
options.D: It cannot be performed using free weights

questions.explanation: A 1-RM test requires the patient to exert one true maximal effort, which is unsafe for patients with joint impairments, those recovering from or at risk of soft tissue injury, or those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology — alternative methods (e.g. multiple-RM formulas, dynamometry, percentage of body weight) are used instead for these patients.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Repetition Maximum, Precautions

questions.question: For a typical healthy but untrained adult beginning a resistance training program, the recommended training zone (percentage of baseline RM) generally falls between:
questions.explanation: For healthy but untrained adults, a typical training zone falls between 40% and 70% of the baseline RM, with the lower end of the range safer at the start of a program to focus on correct form before progressing intensity.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: What is the general relationship between the intensity (load) of resistance exercise and the number of repetitions/sets possible?

options.A: There is no relationship — repetitions are independent of load
options.B: An inverse relationship: higher intensity/load permits fewer repetitions and sets, and lower load permits more
options.C: A direct relationship: higher load always allows more repetitions
options.D: Repetitions only depend on the patient's age, never on the load used

questions.explanation: There is an inverse relationship between exercise intensity (load) and the number of repetitions/sets possible — the higher the load, the fewer repetitions and sets that can be performed, and vice versa.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: Training to improve muscular (local) endurance typically involves:

options.A: A very heavy load for only 1-2 repetitions
options.B: Many repetitions (e.g. 3-5 sets of 40-50 reps) against a low, submaximal load
options.C: A single maximal isometric contraction held for 1 second
options.D: Complete rest with no muscular activity

questions.explanation: Muscle endurance training involves performing many repetitions against a submaximal load — for example, as many as three to five sets of 40 to 50 repetitions against a low resistance — and can be safely initiated early in rehabilitation since the load involved is low.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — To Improve Muscle Endurance

questions.question: When a muscle is immobilized after injury, which muscle fiber type atrophies at a FASTER rate, and what is the clinical implication?

options.A: Type II (fast twitch) fibers atrophy faster, so power training should be prioritized immediately
options.B: Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster, contributing to faster atrophy of antigravity muscles and underscoring the need for early endurance training
options.C: Both fiber types atrophy at exactly the same rate with immobilization
options.D: Immobilization has no effect on muscle fiber composition

questions.explanation: With immobilization, Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster than Type II (fast twitch) fibers, and there is also a slow-to-fast fiber type conversion with disuse. Since antigravity (postural) muscles rely heavily on Type I fibers, this contributes to their faster rate of atrophy compared to their antagonists — supporting early initiation of endurance-type training after injury or surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Muscle Fiber Atrophy

questions.question: When multiple muscle groups are exercised in a single session, the recommended order is generally:

options.A: Small muscle groups before large muscle groups, single-joint before multi-joint exercises
options.B: Large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises
options.C: Order makes no difference to fatigue or training effect
options.D: Lower intensity exercises should always precede higher intensity ones, regardless of warm-up

questions.explanation: The recommended exercise order is large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises, with higher-intensity exercises performed before lower-intensity ones after an appropriate warm-up.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: Following moderate-intensity resistance training, what rest period is generally recommended between sets?

options.D: No rest is needed between sets

questions.explanation: For moderate-intensity resistance training, a 2- to 3-minute rest period between sets is generally recommended, with longer rest periods (>3 minutes) needed for high-intensity training of large, multi-joint muscle groups.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: When the velocity of a limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device during exercise, this is referred to as:
questions.explanation: An isokinetic contraction is one where the velocity of limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device (an isokinetic dynamometer), distinguishing it from standard dynamic (isotonic) exercise where velocity is not controlled.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Type of Muscle Contraction

questions.question: Closed-chain exercise is best described as exercise performed:

options.A: In a nonweight-bearing position with the distal segment moving freely
options.B: In a weight-bearing position where the body moves over a fixed distal segment
options.C: Only using free weights, never body weight

questions.explanation: Closed-chain exercise is performed in a weight-bearing position, where the body moves over a relatively fixed distal segment (e.g. the foot on the ground during a squat). Open-chain exercise, by contrast, is performed nonweight-bearing, with the distal segment (hand or foot) moving freely.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Position for Exercise

questions.question: During a maximum-effort CONCENTRIC muscle contraction, what happens to the force a muscle can generate as the velocity of shortening increases?

options.B: Force decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases
options.C: Force remains completely constant regardless of velocity
options.D: Force becomes unmeasurable at any velocity above zero

questions.explanation: For a maximal concentric contraction, force output decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases — the muscle has less time to develop peak tension at higher shortening velocities. This is opposite to the pattern often seen with eccentric contractions, where force initially rises with velocity before leveling off.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: Early strength gains observed in the first 2-3 weeks of a resistance training program are primarily attributed to:

options.B: Neural adaptation, since significant hypertrophy/vascularization changes typically require at least 6-12 weeks
options.C: An increase in the total number of muscle fibers (hyperplasia)

questions.explanation: Strength gains in the first 2-3 weeks of resistance training are mainly the result of neural adaptation (improved motor unit recruitment and coordination), not muscle tissue change. Significant hypertrophy or increased vascularization typically requires at least 6-12 weeks of consistent training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques

questions.question: In periodized training, the 'competition' phase is generally characterized by:

options.A: Lower loads and the highest number of repetitions and sets
options.B: Higher loads (peaking just prior to competition), with fewer exercises per session and reduced volume compared to the preparation phase
options.D: Only aerobic exercise, no resistance training

questions.explanation: In periodized training, the competition phase uses higher loads peaking just before competition, along with fewer exercises per session and decreased repetitions/sets compared to the earlier preparation phase, which uses lower loads and higher volume.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Periodization and Variation of Training
